Appendix B Particle Transport

Particle transport describes the evolution of particles undergoing scattering and absorption within a medium. The spatial, angular, and energy distribution of particles is governed by the steady-state linear Boltzmann transport equation. Let ψ⁡(𝐱,ω,E)\psi(\mathbf{x},\omega,E) denote the angular particle density at position 𝐱\mathbf{x}, direction ω∈𝕊\omega\in\mathbb{S}, and energy EE. The transport equation reads

ω⋅∇𝐱ψ​(𝐱,ω,E)+σt​(𝐱,E)​ψ​(𝐱,ω,E)\displaystyle\omega\cdot\nabla_{\mathbf{x}}\psi(\mathbf{x},\omega,E)+\mathbf{\sigma}_{t}(\mathbf{x},E)\psi(\mathbf{x},\omega,E) =Q⁡(𝐱,ω,E)\displaystyle=Q(\mathbf{x},\omega,E)
+∫0∞∫𝕊σs𝐟s(𝐱,E′→E,ω′→ω)ψ(𝐱,ω′,E′)dω′dE′\displaystyle+\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{\mathbb{S}}\mathbf{\sigma}_{s}\mathbf{f}_{s}(\mathbf{x},E^{\prime}\rightarrow E,\omega^{\prime}\rightarrow\omega)\psi(\mathbf{x},\omega^{\prime},E^{\prime})\mathrm{d}\omega^{\prime}\mathrm{d}E^{\prime}

Here QQ is the source term, σt\mathbf{\sigma}_{t} is the total cross section (the probability per unit path length that a particle interacts), σs\mathbf{\sigma}_{s} is the scattering cross section (the same probability for scattering alone), and 𝐟s\mathbf{f}_{s} is the scattering function; all three are properties of the material the particle is interacting with. Applications usually require a lower-dimensional response, such as detector flux, surface current, or image radiance, rather than the full angular density ψ\psi. We denote this response by 𝒰⁡(a)\mathcal{U}(a) and express it as a linear functional of ψ\psi. We write

𝒰⁡(a)=∫d​E​∫d​ω​∫d​𝐱​χ​(𝐱,ω,E)​ψ​(𝐱,ω,E)\displaystyle\mathcal{U}(a)=\int\mathrm{d}E\int\mathrm{d}\omega\int\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}\,\,\chi(\mathbf{x},\omega,E)\psi(\mathbf{x},\omega,E) (18)

where χ⁡(𝐱,ω,E)\chi(\mathbf{x},\omega,E) is a test function encoding the measurement process (e.g., detector response, surface current, or volume flux), and aa denotes the input configuration, including geometry, material properties, and source parameters.

The same response can be viewed as an expectation over simulated particle trajectories, each contributing to image radiance or a neutron-flux tally. The path-space integral below expresses this average over trajectories. Let ξ∈Ω\xi\in\Omega denote a particle path consisting of a sequence of free-flight segments and scattering events, and let Ω=∪k≥1Ωk\Omega=\cup_{k\geq 1}\Omega_{k} be the space of all paths grouped by the number of scattering events kk. The measurable response can be written as

𝒰⁡(a)=∫Ωf⁡(ξ,a)​𝑑ν​(ξ),\displaystyle\mathcal{U}(a)=\int_{\Omega}f(\xi,a)\mathrm{d}\nu(\xi), (19)

where ν\nu is the underlying path-space measure induced by the transport process. The contribution function f⁡(ξ,a)f(\xi,a) encodes the accumulated weight of a particle trajectory ξ\xi, including emission at the source, attenuation along free-flight segments, and scattering events along the path. More concretely, for a path ξ=(𝐱0→𝐱1→⋯→𝐱k)\xi=(\mathbf{x}_{0}\to\mathbf{x}_{1}\to\cdots\to\mathbf{x}_{k}) with kk scattering events, ff takes the form of a product of source, transmittance, and scattering terms derived from the transport equation:

f⁡(ξ,a)∝Q⁡(𝐱0→𝐱1)​[∏j=0k−1τ⁡(𝐱j→𝐱j+1)]​∏j=1k−1[σs​(𝐱j+1)​𝐟s​(𝐱j−1→𝐱j→𝐱j+1)]​χ​(𝐱k),\displaystyle f(\xi,a)\propto Q(\mathbf{x}_{0}\rightarrow\mathbf{x}_{1})[\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}\tau(\mathbf{x}_{j}\rightarrow\mathbf{x}_{j+1})]\prod_{j=1}^{k-1}\left[\,\mathbf{\sigma}_{s}(\mathbf{x}_{j+1})\,\mathbf{f}_{s}(\mathbf{x}_{j-1}\rightarrow\mathbf{x}_{j}\rightarrow\mathbf{x}_{j+1})\,\right]\,\chi(\mathbf{x}_{k}), (20)

where τ\tau denotes the transmittance along each segment, which depends on the total cross section σt\mathbf{\sigma}_{t}, and χ\chi encodes the measurement response. This formulation is equivalent to the integral form of the Boltzmann equation.

Monte Carlo methods approximate this integral by sampling NN paths ξi∼p(⋅∣a)\xi_{i}\sim p(\cdot\mid a) from a proposal distribution pp and collecting them in ξ=(ξ1,…,ξN)\xi=(\xi_{1},\ldots,\xi_{N}). The estimator is given by

𝒰^N​(a,ξ)=1N​∑i=1Nf⁡(ξi,a)p⁡(ξi∣a).\displaystyle\hat{\mathcal{U}}_{N}(a,\xi)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{f(\xi_{i},a)}{p(\xi_{i}\mid a)}. (21)

With a proposal that covers all contributing paths and the corresponding importance weights f/pf/p, this estimator is unbiased. Its variance can be high in multiple-scattering or shielding regimes because only a small fraction of sampled histories contribute appreciably to the response. Sampling paths in proportion to their contribution would reduce this variance, but constructing such a distribution requires knowing which complete trajectories contribute most before tracing them. As a result, obtaining low-noise estimates of 𝒰⁡(a)\mathcal{U}(a) requires a large number of samples, making data generation expensive.

Appendix C Loss Definitions and Engineering Stabilizers

Output head.

The PTNO output head ℬθ​(a)=softplus⁡(𝒢θ​(a))\mathcal{B}_{\theta}(a)=\operatorname{softplus}(\mathcal{G}_{\theta}(a)) is the default everywhere in the main paper; we use softplus⁡(s)=ln⁡(1+es)\operatorname{softplus}(s)=\ln(1+e^{s}), which is smooth, monotone, and nonnegative, asymptotically linear for s≫0s\!\gg\!0 and decays smoothly to zero for s≪0s\!\ll\!0. Its derivative ∂ssoftplus⁡(s)=1/(1+e−s)≤1\partial_{s}\operatorname{softplus}(s)=1/(1+e^{-s})\leq 1 already bounds the per-voxel gradient.

Floors.

We use small positive floors in two places: a stop-gradient denominator floor η\eta in the training residual (section 4), and a log-metric floor ϵ\epsilon when reporting log10\log_{10} metrics. The paper reports log10⁡(max⁡(⋅,ϵ))\log_{10}(\max(\cdot,\epsilon)) metrics with the task floors in Table 4 (all metric definitions are in Appendix ); for EU-DEMO, the post-hoc checkpoint evaluation floors both prediction and reference at ϵ=10−17\epsilon=10^{-17}.

Where the linear error lives on 3D fluence.

The linear rel. L2L_{2} of the 3D fluence models is dominated by the voxels around the point emitters, not by the emitter voxel alone. Re-scoring the five PTNO seeds of Table 2 on the 100100 held-out scenes with the emitter voxels excluded (2.02.0 voxels per scene on average) removes only 35%35\% of the squared error (mean over scenes; 30%30\% median), whereas excluding the 3×3×33{\times}3{\times}3 core around each emitter (5454 voxels, 0.02%0.02\% of the grid) removes 95.0%95.0\% and lowers the mean rel. L2L_{2} from 2.11±1.412.11\pm 1.41 to 0.270±0.1040.270\pm 0.104 (median over scenes 0.301±0.0300.301\pm 0.030 to 0.182±0.0180.182\pm 0.018). The emitter voxel itself is a grid convention with no continuum limit (its cell average scales as h−2h^{-2} with the voxel width hh), but its neighbors are converged field values, so the remaining near-source error is a genuine model error; the mean is inflated by a handful of scenes per seed with rel. L2L_{2} above one, and the log-space metrics, which are unaffected by this concentration, are the ones we rank by.

PRel​L2\mathrm{PRel}L_{2} normalizer.

For PTNO targets the PRel​L2\mathrm{PRel}L_{2} normalizes the residual by the prediction itself, with the gradient on the denominator detached:

ri​(a,ξ)=[ℬθ​(a)]i−𝒰^N,i​(a,ξ)sg⁡(max⁡([ℬθ​(a)]i,η)),r_{i}(a,\xi)\;=\;\frac{[\mathcal{B}_{\theta}(a)]_{i}-\hat{\mathcal{U}}_{N,i}(a,\xi)}{\operatorname{sg}\!\big(\max([\mathcal{B}_{\theta}(a)]_{i},\,\eta)\big)}, (22)

where sg⁡(⋅)\operatorname{sg}(\cdot) blocks gradient flow through the normalizer. The denominator floor caps the per-voxel gradient magnitude when [ℬθ]i[\mathcal{B}_{\theta}]_{i} underestimates the target by many orders of magnitude.

Per-experiment instantiations.

Table 4 lists the reported log-metric floor ϵ\epsilon used per experiment. All entries use the softplus head and the PRel​L2\mathrm{PRel}L_{2} residual of Equation (22); no model-side clamp or robust-loss transition is active.

The floor never binds on far-field radiance, whose references stay above 10−610^{-6}; on 3D fluence, the spherical tokamak, and EU-DEMO it removes the deepest 1.61.6, 2.02.0, and 6.16.1 orders of magnitude of the mean reference span (Table 18). On EU-DEMO, voxels outside the transport domain and voxels the reference never reaches sit exactly on the 10−1710^{-17} floor. analyzes the stationary points of the PRel​L2\mathrm{PRel}L_{2} residual; the EU-DEMO scores in Table 2 exclude these voxels and use only the cells the reference measured.

Reference engines.

Far-field radiance references use Mitsuba 3 [1]; 3D fluence references use the same forward MC estimator as its labels, cross-checked against OpenMC; neutron transport uses OpenMC [2]. Each held-out set is independently rendered to convergence; architecture and schedule details are stated in each subsection.

Appendix D Denominator and Output-Head Ablations

The PRel​L2\mathrm{PRel}L_{2} residual of Equation (22) makes two coupled design choices: the softplus output head and the detached-prediction denominator, i.e., the prediction with its gradient stopped. We isolate both with matched-compute ablations on the 3D fluence and EU-DEMO datasets.

3D fluence: denominator ×\times activation.

Table 5 crosses the output head (softplus vs. raw identity) with four residual denominators (detached prediction, live prediction, plain per-sample relative L2L_{2}, and the noisy MC target) on the 3D fluence dataset (M=3×105M{=}3{\times}10^{5}, N=4N{=}4, 6060 epochs of 5,0005{,}000 scenes, i.e. one pass over the training set, FNO modes 16316^{3}, width 3232; evaluation on 100100 held-out scenes with a converged 1,048,5761{,}048{,}576-SPP reference). The detached-prediction denominator is essential: with a live prediction denominator, through which gradients flow, the loss is flat wherever the prediction overshoots (gradient ∝\propto target/pred2), so training either inflates its output (softplus: total flux ∼15×{\sim}15\times too high and linear rel. L2≈500L_{2}{\approx}500) or collapses to a negative constant field (identity). With the noisy target in the denominator, zero-flux voxels in the N=4N{=}4 labels are divided by the 10−1010^{-10} denominator floor, which amplifies their residuals by up to ten orders of magnitude The softplus head, in turn, only helps when paired with the pointwise stop-gradient residual (first two rows); paired with a per-sample norm ratio it reproduces the absorbing softplus⁡(−∞)=0\operatorname{softplus}(-\infty)=0 fixed point. The plain-FNO variant (identity head, per-sample norm) wins the linear median (it directly optimizes that metric) but loses the entire shadow region in log space.

EU-DEMO: head ×\times pointwise residual.

Prediction normalization is the dominant component on EU-DEMO. Holding the softplus head fixed, replacing PRel​L2\mathrm{PRel}L_{2} with per-sample relative L2L_{2} lowers log10\log_{10} SSIM by 0.37880.3788 and raises its seed standard deviation from 0.00160.0016 to 0.11810.1181. Holding PRel​L2\mathrm{PRel}L_{2} fixed, replacing softplus with an identity head lowers SSIM by 0.08450.0845. The normalization establishes accuracy and seed stability; softplus supplies an additional SSIM gain and enforces positive flux.

Appendix E Datasets

Table 7summarizes the four datasets of the main text; Appendix K adds a fifth.

E.1 Radiative Transfer in a Spherical Slab

The medium is the unit ball {𝐱:‖𝐱‖≤1}\{\mathbf{x}:\|\mathbf{x}\|\leq 1\}. Inside it, the extinction σt\mathbf{\sigma}_{t} and single-scattering albedo cc depend only on the line-of-sight direction 𝐱^=𝐱/‖𝐱‖\hat{\mathbf{x}}=\mathbf{x}/\|\mathbf{x}\|, defined analytically and tabulated on arccos-uniform spherical grids (equal solid-angle bins in the polar angle ϑ\vartheta, ϑi=arccos⁡(1−2​(i+12)/nϑ)\vartheta_{i}=\arccos(1-2(i+\tfrac{1}{2})/n_{\vartheta}) for nϑn_{\vartheta} polar bins; ×8040\!\times\!80 for training inputs). Anisotropic scattering uses a Henyey–Greenstein phase function with one asymmetry parameter g∈(−0.99,0.99)g\in(-0.99,0.99) per scene. The source is an environment map Q⁡(ω)Q(\omega) at infinity; the boundary is a null interface, so light enters without refraction or reflection. A reference spans only about 33 orders of magnitude (Table 18): this dataset is a controlled testbed for label noise and particle-budget allocation, where converged references are affordable, not a high-dynamic-range case.

Sampling.

Each scene draws three resolution-independent analytical fields plus one scalar. The source combines 11–44 spherical Gaussian lobes (angular width in [0.15,0.5][0.15,0.5], random centers) with 11–44 boxes in polar and azimuthal angle (ϑ,φ)(\vartheta,\varphi), each carrying an intensity drawn from [0.1,10][0.1,10]. Extinction and albedo are piecewise-constant Heaviside fields: with probability 12\tfrac{1}{2} a spherical checkerboard (11–33 polar ×\times 11–66 azimuthal bins), otherwise 11–66 random (ϑ,φ)(\vartheta,\varphi) boxes, with values drawn from σt∈[0.01,10]\mathbf{\sigma}_{t}\in[0.01,10] and c∈[0.01,0.99]c\in[0.01,0.99]. Because the fields are analytical, the discontinuous region boundaries are represented exactly at every rendering resolution. The HG parameter is g∼Unif⁡(−0.99,0.99)g\!\sim\!\mathrm{Unif}(-0.99,0.99).

Reference.

Evaluation references use Mitsuba 3’s volumetric path tracer with multiple importance sampling [1], and the training labels are forward MC estimates of the same scenes: a sphere boundary (null BSDF) encloses a heterogeneous medium that reads (σt,c)(\mathbf{\sigma}_{t},c) from the angular tables, an HG phase function with parameter gg, and an environment-map emitter carrying the equirectangular source bitmap (resampled to the Mitsuba Y-up convention). A distant angular sensor records the far-field radiance on the same arccos-uniform ×8040\!\times\!80 grid. Training: 10610^{6} scenes with K=1K\!=\!1 renders at 44 SPP (Monte Carlo samples per pixel of the ×8040\!\times\!80 sensor) each. Evaluation: 100100 unseen scenes rendered at native ×240120\!\times\!240 with ×1,920960\!\times\!1{,}920 material and environment textures, accumulated adaptively until convergence (per-pixel coefficient of variation <0.5%<\!0.5\% and successive-mean rel. L2<10−4L_{2}\!<\!10^{-4}) or a 10710^{7} SPP cap; the ×8040\!\times\!80 and ×16080\!\times\!160 evaluation grids are conservative equal-solid-angle downsamples of these renders. An earlier fixed-budget 10510^{5} SPP reference on the same 100100 scenes, used for earlier loss-comparison tables, agrees with the converged reference to a median per-scene rel. L2L_{2} of 1.9%1.9\%; re-evaluating the checkpoints that are still available against the converged reference moves the main metrics by 11–2%2\% relative. Figure 5 shows one converged scene next to a training-budget render and the PTNO prediction.

E.2 3D Fluence

The medium occupies [−1,1]3[-1,1]^{3} in scene units, discretized on a 64364^{3} Cartesian grid. Each scene is built from resolution-independent ingredients: 22–55 large axis-aligned boxes in a near-vacuum background (σt=0.01\mathbf{\sigma}_{t}=0.01, c=0.5c=0.5), each box carrying its own extinction σt\mathbf{\sigma}_{t} and albedo cc, and 11–33 point emitters at random positions. About half of the emitters are isotropic; the others carry a random Perlin angular emission profile in a random orientation. Anisotropic scattering uses an HG phase function with one gg per scene. The boundary is an open vacuum.

Sampling.

Per scene: box centers Unif​(−0.6,0.6)3\mathrm{Unif}(-0.6,0.6)^{3} and half-extents Unif⁡(0.1,0.7)\mathrm{Unif}(0.1,0.7) per axis, with σt∼Unif⁡(0.01,50)\mathbf{\sigma}_{t}\!\sim\!\mathrm{Unif}(0.01,50) and c∼Unif⁡(0.01,0.99)c\!\sim\!\mathrm{Unif}(0.01,0.99) drawn per box and later boxes overwriting earlier ones where they overlap; emitter positions Unif​(−0.85,0.85)3\mathrm{Unif}(-0.85,0.85)^{3} and intensity Unif⁡(1,20)\mathrm{Unif}(1,20), with a Perlin angular profile (values in [0.1,2][0.1,2]) on each emitter with probability 1/21/2; g∼Unif⁡(−0.95,0.95)g\!\sim\!\mathrm{Unif}(-0.95,0.95). The 100100 evaluation scenes realize g∈[−0.92,0.93]g\in[-0.92,0.93].

Reference.

All renders use a forward Monte Carlo collision estimator with double-precision per-voxel accumulators (necessary for HDR), cross-checked against OpenMC [2] on the evaluation scenes. Training: 300,000300{,}000 scenes with K=2K{=}2 independent noisy renders at 44 SPP each, i.e., 44 Monte Carlo samples per voxel of the 64364^{3} grid (∼106\sim\!10^{6} particles per render—a deliberately weak supervision regime that exercises the loss family at extreme noise). Evaluation: a held-out batch of 100100 unseen scenes whose reference flux is re-rendered to ∼106\sim\!10^{6} SPP (∼×1011\sim\!2.7\!\times\!10^{11} particles per scene, ∼×105\sim\!2.6\!\times\!10^{5} times one training render). The reference fluence of a scene spans about 1010 orders of magnitude (Table 18); over the 100100 evaluation scenes, 2.3%2.3\% of reference voxels are exact zeros that no particle reaches even at the reference budget (cast shadows), against 18%18\% in a four-SPP training render (both means over scenes).

E.3 Spherical-Tokamak Neutronics

Each scene is a full toroidal fusion spherical tokamak built parametrically with Paramak using a 6-axis radial build (center-column shield inner/outer radius, blanket thickness, divertor width) plus major and minor radius [40]. The geometry is configured with a plasma source expressed as toroidal rings, radially weighted as a function of fusion reactivity in an H-mode configuration [42]. The CAD assembly is voxelized and tagged with five materials (vacuum, plain-carbon shield, ferritic steel first wall and vessel, Pb–Li breeder blanket). The bounding box, a cube of side 1,8001{,}800 cm, is voxelized on a 64364^{3} Cartesian mesh; the per-voxel material id is queried from the OpenMC geometry, giving a volumetric label that conditions the operator. The prediction target is the raw OpenMC flux-tally mean in each energy group, in neutron-cm per source neutron, integrated over each mesh cell and without conversion to a reactor source rate.

Sampling.

The 20 scalar parameters in Table 8 are drawn from Latin-hypercube space-filling designs over the box specified there: 4 paramak radial-build axes, the four D-shape descriptors (R0,ap,κ,δ)(R_{0},a_{\mathrm{p}},\kappa,\delta) shared between the paramak surface and the H-mode plasma source [42] (D–T fusion ring), 10 axes for the peaked ion-density and ion-temperature profiles (origin, pedestal/separatrix fractions, peaking factor, pedestal radius fraction, temperature exponent β\beta) together with a Shafranov shift of the magnetic axis, and a rigid radial offset of the whole source. The 8 geometry parameters are drawn once per group of 3232 consecutive training configurations, which share one CAD model, while the source parameters are drawn per configuration; the source offset has its own one-dimensional design.

Training and reference.

The training pool has 1,024,0001{,}024{,}000 configurations, each labeled by one OpenMC fixed-source run of N=105N{=}10^{5} histories (1010 batches of 10410^{4}); training draws 4×1054\times 10^{5} of them without repetition (10510^{5} optimizer updates at batch size 44). The 5050 held-out configurations carry a 10910^{9}-history reference pooled from 100100 independent 10710^{7}-history runs; its residual noise is 0.0170.017 in log10\log_{10} relative L2L_{2}, against 0.0450.045 for the operator. The operator is a 3D FNO (modes 24324^{3}, width 3232, 44 layers) trained for 10510^{5} optimizer updates.

E.4 EU-DEMO 1/16 Sector

The fourth dataset uses an OpenMC model over a 1/16 toroidal slice of the EU-DEMO reactor [43]. Sector neutronics models of this kind are widely used in fusion analysis because they retain the main blanket, vessel, shielding, and source-transport physics of a reactor-scale configuration while exploiting toroidal symmetry to reduce computational cost. They are a standard setting for studies of neutron flux distribution, nuclear heating, shielding performance, activation, and diagnostic response in DEMO-like designs.

The geometry of the reactor is modeled using a CSG geometry of about 5,3005{,}300 surfaces (planes, quadrics, cylinders, tori, and cones) [21, 41]. The surfaces describing the inboard/outboard blanket modules, divertor, vacuum vessel, and shielding, are closed by two reflective planes at ±11.25∘\pm 11.25^{\circ} and a vacuum plane at z=−2,732z={-}2{,}732 cm. Materials use the upstream physics-resolved compositions (water-cooled lithium–lead blanket, Eurofer first wall and vessel, etc.) with TENDL-2019 nuclear cross-section data. Geometry, materials, and reactor configuration are fixed across the dataset; only the plasma source varies.

Sampling.

The 8 plasma-source shape parameters in Table 9 are drawn from a Latin-hypercube space-filling design over the upstream ranges of the EU-DEMO parametric plasma source (PPS) configuration.

Reference.

The neutron source is a parametric D–T plasma source parameterized by the 8 plasma-shape variables above together with the wedge angles. The emitted neutron energy is modeled as a thermally broadened 14.1 MeV D–T fusion spectrum, with broadening controlled by the ion temperature. The source is broadly similar in spirit to the more general confinement-mode-dependent source models described by [44], but uses a reduced geometric parameterization and a simplified spectral model. Per scene we (i) voxelize the source onto the flux-tally mesh, so that the operator input and output share a coordinate frame, and (ii) run OpenMC continuous-energy fixed-source transport with neutron-flux mesh tallies on a trimmed 140×73×146140\times 73\times 146 Cartesian mesh. The prediction target is the OpenMC flux-tally mean divided by the mesh-cell volume, in neutrons per square centimeter per source neutron, without conversion to a reactor source rate. The 2424 held-out configurations use a reference computed at 700×365×730700\times 365\times 730 with FW-CADIS and MAGIC weight windows, a median of 6,1306{,}130 core-hours per configuration, and conservatively block-averaged to the 7070, 140140, and 280280 grids used for evaluation. Figure 9 shows the wedge geometry and a representative scene.

Training.

M=105M{=}10^{5} configurations from the sampling design above, each labeled by one OpenMC run of N=5×105N{=}5\times 10^{5} histories on the 140×73×146140\times 73\times 146 mesh (K=1K{=}1). The backbone is a 3D FNO (modes 32×24×3832\times 24\times 38, width 3232, 44 layers, 6.3×1076.3\times 10^{7} parameters) that reads a four-class material-density geometry channel and the 8 source parameters as NeRF-embedded scalars (3737 input channels). Every EU-DEMO model in Table 2 trains with AdamW (learning rate 10−310^{-3}, no weight decay, gradient clipping at 1.01.0) at batch size 11 with 44-step gradient accumulation for two passes over the 10510^{5} configurations, that is 5×1045\times 10^{4} optimizer updates under a cosine schedule that reaches zero at the last update, taking about 2.92.9 hours per run on one H200. Log-space metrics use a floor of 10−1710^{-17} for both predictions and references.

Appendix F Explicit Debiasers for Log-Space Training

Setup.

The single-seed and earlier-model figures below retain their historical checkpoints. Tables 10 and 12 use the new fixed-schedule final checkpoints; the remaining diagnostics await replacement. We confirm the log10\log_{10}-target Jensen bias under two configurations: Setup A (single scene, M=1M{=}1, 5 seeds, labels of one 44-SPP render) and Setup B (multi-scene, M=106M{=}10^{6} train / M=100M{=}100 test, 6 seeds, labels averaging 2020 four-SPP renders, i.e. 8080 SPP), both for 10510^{5} optimization steps. Figures 10 and 11 show that log MSE converges to a strictly higher validation rel. L2L_{2} than a model trained in physical space (an earlier version of our method: a physical-space L2L_{2} loss on a 10𝒢θ10^{\mathcal{G}_{\theta}} output head, without the softplus head and the pointwise normalization of PRel​L2\mathrm{PRel}L_{2}), and that an NO trained against log10⁡𝒰^N​(a,ξ)\log_{10}\!\hat{\mathcal{U}}_{N}(a,\xi) systematically under-predicts the solution by the empirical Jensen offset.

Stratified loss comparison.

Table 10 stratifies % RMSE and log10\log_{10} SSIM by reference brightness across the 100100 held-out far-field scenes, for the five-seed far-field models of Table 2. Log MSE underperforms PTNO + PRel​L2\mathrm{PRel}L_{2} in every bin; L2L_{2} on raw NO output loses contrast in dim regions (log10\log_{10} SSIM 0.240.24 in the dimmest bin and at most 0.780.78 in any bin); PTNO + PRel​L2\mathrm{PRel}L_{2} keeps log10\log_{10} SSIM between 0.890.89 and 0.940.94 across all four brightness bins. This table does not separate the contributions of the softplus head and the PRel​L2\mathrm{PRel}L_{2} residual to the dim-bin improvement; Appendix D does.

Explicit log-target debiasers.

The log MSE row in Table 1 suffers Jensen bias because 𝔼⁡[log10⁡𝒰^N]≠log10⁡𝔼⁡[𝒰^N]\mathbb{E}\!\left[\log_{10}\hat{\mathcal{U}}_{N}\right]\neq\log_{10}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\hat{\mathcal{U}}_{N}\right] at finite NN. A natural fix is to construct an explicitly debiased or lower-bias log10\log_{10}-target estimator from KK independent renders and feed that into a standard log-space MSE. We compare three such estimators against PRel​L2\mathrm{PRel}L_{2} trained with the exponential output head 10𝒢θ10^{\mathcal{G}_{\theta}} of an earlier model version:

  • •

    Log of mean (K=10K{=}10): the log10\log_{10} of the average of 1010 available 44-SPP renders, equivalent in expectation to one 4040-SPP render.

  • •

    Second-moment correction (K=10K{=}10): log10⁡Y¯K+σ^2/(2​K​Y¯K2​ln⁡10)\log_{10}\bar{Y}_{K}+\widehat{\sigma}^{2}/(2K\bar{Y}_{K}^{2}\ln 10) where the same KK renders are used to estimate the mean and variance.

  • •

    Taylor fallback (5+55{+}5): a Taylor–Russian-roulette log estimator with a second-moment fallback on high-coefficient-of-variation pixels.

Implementation of the log-target debiasers.

All log-target debiasers are applied independently at every output pixel to the stored stack of repeated 44-SPP renders for the same scene. Let Y1,…,YKY_{1},\ldots,Y_{K} denote the selected independent renders, let Y¯K=K−1​∑iYi\bar{Y}_{K}=K^{-1}\sum_{i}Y_{i}, and let ϵ=10−6\epsilon=10^{-6} be the same floor used by the far-field evaluation. The log-of-mean target is

z^mean=log10⁡(max⁡(Y¯10,ϵ)).\widehat{z}_{\mathrm{mean}}=\log_{10}\!\left(\max(\bar{Y}_{10},\epsilon)\right).

The second-moment row uses the delta-method correction

z^2​n​d=1ln⁡10​[ln⁡(max⁡(Y¯10,ϵ))+σ^22​K​max⁡(Y¯10,ϵ)2],\widehat{z}_{\mathrm{2nd}}=\frac{1}{\ln 10}\left[\ln\!\left(\max(\bar{Y}_{10},\epsilon)\right)+\frac{\widehat{\sigma}^{2}}{2K\max(\bar{Y}_{10},\epsilon)^{2}}\right],

where σ^2\widehat{\sigma}^{2} is the unbiased sample variance of the same K=10K{=}10 renders. The Taylor fallback row splits the selected renders into 55 anchor renders and 55 correction renders. The anchor group forms μ^=max⁡(15​∑i=15Yi,ϵ)\hat{\mu}=\max(\frac{1}{5}\sum_{i=1}^{5}Y_{i},\epsilon). For correction render Y5+jY_{5+j}, j=1,…,5j=1,\ldots,5, define rj=(Y5+j−μ^)/μ^r_{j}=(Y_{5+j}-\hat{\mu})/\hat{\mu}. The estimator uses product terms from the Taylor series of the log of the pixel mean μ=𝔼⁡[Yi]\mu=\mathbb{E}[Y_{i}]

ln⁡μ=ln⁡μ^+∑m≥1(−1)m+1m​(μ−μ^μ^)m,\ln\mu=\ln\hat{\mu}+\sum_{m\geq 1}\frac{(-1)^{m+1}}{m}\left(\frac{\mu-\hat{\mu}}{\hat{\mu}}\right)^{m},

with ∏j=1mrj\prod_{j=1}^{m}r_{j} estimating the mmth power term. We average 3232 Russian-roulette paths, i.e., randomly truncated series whose surviving terms are reweighted by their survival probability, with continuation probability qm=min⁡(CV​m/(m+1),0.95)q_{m}=\min(\mathrm{CV}\,m/(m+1),0.95), where CV is the coefficient of variation estimated from the selected renders. Pixels with CV≥1\mathrm{CV}\geq 1 or non-finite roulette output fall back to the second-moment estimator above. These procedures debias the transformed target as much as possible under the K=10K{=}10 render budget, but the resulting training objective is still ordinary log-space MSE; the KK extra renders are amortized over the training set, not the stochastic gradient.

Table 11 reports metrics averaged over the 100100 held-out scenes against the naive baseline at N=4N{=}4; each debiaser cuts the naive-log % RMSE by 5050–59%59\%, but none closes the gap to PRel​L2\mathrm{PRel}L_{2}, shown here with the exponential 10𝒢θ10^{\mathcal{G}_{\theta}} output head of an earlier model version rather than the softplus head of PTNO.

Each explicit debiaser cuts the naive-log % RMSE by 5050–59%59\%, but none achieves performance comparable to training the model with our proposed loss, even though they require extra renders. The gap is widest in log10\log_{10} rel. L2L_{2}, where ours reaches 0.0830.083 versus 0.4560.456 for the next best (2nd-moment MSE, K=10K{=}10).

Appendix G Bias Correction for Target-Denominator relL2L_{2}

Figure 13 and Table 12 study how Jensen bias affects relative-L2L_{2} training on the far-field radiance dataset. The baseline relL2L_{2} objective uses noisy MC labels in the denominator, so the nonlinear reciprocal-square map moves the empirical minimizer away from the physical solution. We compare that baseline with two relL2L_{2} bias-correction strategies that estimate the inverse-square scale from extra independent renders, and with our pointwise relative loss. The bias-corrected relL2L_{2} variants reduce the collapse but still land far worse than PTNO + PRel​L2\mathrm{PRel}L_{2}. This appendix documents the full definitions of the corresponding losses.

Why the label denominator cannot be repaired.

The weak labels put a point mass at zero, so the inverse-square weight of the label-denominator loss has no finite expectation (Table 13). About 15%15\% of the pixels of a ten-render mean are exactly zero, and their weights reach ∼1012{\sim}10^{12} against ∼2×102{\sim}2\times 10^{2} for a typical (median) pixel of the same label (∼2×104{\sim}2\times 10^{4} for a single render). The loss then reduces to reproducing zeros where the label is zero, the optimizer drives the whole field to the softplus floor, and the vanishing gradient there prevents recovery, which is the first-epoch collapse behind the baseline row of Table 12 and panel (b) of Figure 13. Any repair, such as a label floor or a mask on zero pixels, changes the target rather than removing the bias.

Implementation of the relL2L_{2} bias corrections.

PTNO + PRel​L2\mathrm{PRel}L_{2} uses a 1010-render target mean Y¯10\bar{Y}_{10}, i.e., a 4040-SPP effective target, but its denominator is the prediction:

ℓsg=(Bθ−Y¯10max⁡(sg⁡(Bθ),η))2,Bθ=softplus⁡(𝒢θ​(a)).\ell_{\mathrm{sg}}=\left(\frac{B_{\theta}-\bar{Y}_{10}}{\max(\operatorname{sg}(B_{\theta}),\eta)}\right)^{2},\qquad B_{\theta}=\operatorname{softplus}(\mathcal{G}_{\theta}(a)).

Conditioned on the prediction, the denominator is a constant and the stochastic gradient remains centered at the physical solution. The baseline relL2L_{2} objective instead puts the same noisy target in the scale,

ℓtgt=(B−Y¯10sg⁡(Y¯10)+η)2.\ell_{\mathrm{tgt}}=\left(\frac{B-\bar{Y}_{10}}{\operatorname{sg}(\bar{Y}_{10})+\eta}\right)^{2}.

For a scalar prediction BB, its stationary point is

B∗=𝔼⁡[Y¯10/(Y¯10+η)2]𝔼⁡[1/(Y¯10+η)2],B^{*}=\frac{\mathbb{E}\!\left[\bar{Y}_{10}/(\bar{Y}_{10}+\eta)^{2}\right]}{\mathbb{E}\!\left[1/(\bar{Y}_{10}+\eta)^{2}\right]},

which is an inverse-MC-weighted target rather than 𝔼⁡[Y¯10]\mathbb{E}[\bar{Y}_{10}].

The two relL2L_{2} bias corrections try to repair this by keeping the residual render independent from the denominator estimate. They train

ℓiw=W^​(Bθ−Yr)2,\ell_{\mathrm{iw}}=\widehat{W}\,(B_{\theta}-Y_{r})^{2},

where YrY_{r} is one selected 44-SPP residual render and W^\widehat{W} is computed from disjoint renders. If W^\widehat{W} were a stable low-variance estimate of (𝔼⁡[Y]+η)−2(\mathbb{E}[Y]+\eta)^{-2}, independence would recover the correct fixed point. The second-order bias correction uses K=10K{=}10 anchor renders with

A¯K=1K​∑i=1KAi,μ^=max⁡(A¯K,η),σ^A2=1K−1​∑i=1K(Ai−A¯K)2.\bar{A}_{K}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{i=1}^{K}A_{i},\qquad\hat{\mu}=\max(\bar{A}_{K},\eta),\qquad\widehat{\sigma}_{A}^{2}=\frac{1}{K-1}\sum_{i=1}^{K}(A_{i}-\bar{A}_{K})^{2}.

For the weight w⁡(x)=(x+η)−2w(x)=(x+\eta)^{-2}, with μ=𝔼⁡[Ai]\mu=\mathbb{E}[A_{i}] and σ2=Var⁡(Ai)\sigma^{2}=\operatorname{Var}(A_{i}), the delta method gives

𝔼⁡[w⁡(A¯K)]≈w⁡(μ)+12​w′′​(μ)​σ2K=(μ+η)−2+3​σ2K​(μ+η)4,\mathbb{E}[w(\bar{A}_{K})]\approx w(\mu)+\frac{1}{2}w^{\prime\prime}(\mu)\frac{\sigma^{2}}{K}=(\mu+\eta)^{-2}+\frac{3\sigma^{2}}{K(\mu+\eta)^{4}},

so the inverse-square analog of the second-moment log correction subtracts this leading plug-in bias:

W^2=[(μ^+η)−2−3​σ^A2K​(μ^+η)4]+.\widehat{W}_{2}=\left[(\hat{\mu}+\eta)^{-2}-\frac{3\widehat{\sigma}_{A}^{2}}{K(\hat{\mu}+\eta)^{4}}\right]_{+}.

The Taylor bias correction splits its 1010 renders into 55 anchor renders AiA_{i} and 55 correction renders Aj′A^{\prime}_{j}. The anchors give a stable expansion point μ^=max⁡(15​∑iAi,η)\hat{\mu}=\max(\frac{1}{5}\sum_{i}A_{i},\eta), and each correction render contributes a mean-zero relative residual rj=(Aj′−μ^)/(μ^+η)r_{j}=(A^{\prime}_{j}-\hat{\mu})/(\hat{\mu}+\eta), which is an unbiased estimator of (μ−μ^)/(μ^+η)(\mu-\hat{\mu})/(\hat{\mu}+\eta). Expanding the inverse-square weight (μ+η)−2(\mu+\eta)^{-2} around μ^\hat{\mu} gives

(μ+η)−2=(μ^+η)−2​∑m≥0(−1)m​(m+1)​(μ−μ^μ^+η)m.(\mu+\eta)^{-2}=(\hat{\mu}+\eta)^{-2}\sum_{m\geq 0}(-1)^{m}(m+1)\left(\frac{\mu-\hat{\mu}}{\hat{\mu}+\eta}\right)^{m}.

Because the rjr_{j} are independent, the product ∏j=1mrj\prod_{j=1}^{m}r_{j} is an unbiased estimator of the mm-th power, so plugging products of fresh residuals into successive series terms preserves unbiasedness. We truncate at m=5m{=}5 (one product per correction render) to obtain the plug-in weight

W^T=(μ^+η)−2​[1+∑m=15(−1)m​(m+1)​∏j=1mrj].\widehat{W}_{\mathrm{T}}=(\hat{\mu}+\eta)^{-2}\left[1+\sum_{m=1}^{5}(-1)^{m}(m+1)\prod_{j=1}^{m}r_{j}\right].

Pixels with maxj⁡|rj|>0.95\max_{j}|r_{j}|>0.95 fall back to the second-order weight; remaining non-finite values are zeroed and the final weights are clamped nonnegative. The raw Taylor–Russian-roulette diagnostic uses the same inverse-power series with 88 roulette paths and continuation qm=min⁡(|r|¯​m/(m+1),0.95)q_{m}=\min(\overline{|r|}\,m/(m+1),0.95), but it produced non-finite weights on the first batch and is therefore not reported as a successful training run.

As with the log-target debiasers in the previous section, the KK extra renders are amortized over the training set, not the stochastic gradient. The bias corrections reduce the most direct denominator-target coupling, but the corrected relL2L_{2} objectives still concentrate optimization on unstable inverse-scale weights and do not recover the prediction-normalized PRel​L2\mathrm{PRel}L_{2} solution. Per-run numbers are tabulated in Table 12.

Appendix H Cost Accounting and Speedup

The EU-DEMO accuracy crossings below use the final checkpoints. The other tasks retain their historical accuracy crossings and timings pending the corresponding reruns; their checkpoint limitations are recorded in Appendix .

The surrogate repays its offline cost after 1212–197197 queries, and at matched accuracy it is 10310^{3}–105×10^{5}\times cheaper than MC on neutronics, while on radiative transfer MC costs 0.80.8–11×11\times the operator. Table 14 summarizes the comparison; the paragraphs below give the offline cost, the same-device comparison against converged MC, and the matched-accuracy measurement.

Offline cost and break-even.

Converged labels for our training sets would cost 5×1035\times 10^{3}–105×10^{5}\times more than the noisy labels we train on (Table 15, “Converged / noisy”). Break-even divides the offline cost, label generation plus training, by the cost of one converged solve minus one inference. For the neutronics tasks, GPU training time is small next to CPU label generation and is listed separately rather than converted to core-hours. Labeling the EU-DEMO training set at converged quality would take ≈6×108{\approx}6\times 10^{8} core-hours.

Same device, converged MC.

Reproducing a converged reference costs MC 1.2×1041.2\times 10^{4}–1.8×105×1.8\times 10^{5}\times the operator’s inference when both run on the same device. Figure 4 times the operator on a GPU and MC on a 24-thread CPU, because OpenMC has no GPU implementation, and that ratio folds a hardware factor of 1010–60×60\times into the comparison; the numbers here remove it. On the same device and the reference’s own output grid, converged MC costs 1.8×105×1.8\times 10^{5}\times (far-field radiance, 607607 s for 2202^{20} SPP on the 40×8040{\times}80 output grid, which reproduces the reference to log10\log_{10} rel. L2L_{2} 0.00080.0008, against 3.43.4 ms) and 1.8×104×1.8\times 10^{4}\times (3D fluence, 2,6362{,}636 s against 144144 ms) the operator’s inference, both methods timed on one RTX 5070 Laptop GPU. On one 24-thread CPU (Xeon Gold 6130 for the spherical tokamak, Xeon Platinum 8352Y for EU-DEMO), the per-scene median is 9.9×104×9.9\times 10^{4}\times for the spherical tokamak (10910^{9} histories against a 0.470.47 s forward pass) and 1.2×104×1.2\times 10^{4}\times for EU-DEMO (the full weight-window and transport chain, median 6,1306{,}130 core-hours, against a 7979 s forward pass on the 700×365×730700\times 365\times 730 reference grid).

Matched accuracy.

MC reaches the operator’s accuracy cheaply on radiative transfer and only at great cost on neutronics. For every held-out scene we sweep the MC budget on the same device, score each budget against an independent reference with the metric used for the operator, and record the cost at which MC first matches the operator’s error; we report the median over scenes. On far-field radiance (100100 scenes), MC matches log10\log_{10} SSIM at 11.3×11.3\times the operator’s cost (interquartile range 4.54.5–3434) and log10\log_{10} relative L2L_{2} at 5.5×5.5\times (3.43.4–10.510.5). On 3D fluence (100100 scenes) the factors are 2.1×2.1\times (1.01.0–9.69.6) and 0.8×0.8\times (0.440.44–2.22.2): MC matches the norm error within the operator’s own inference time on half of the scenes. On the spherical tokamak (5050 scenes), we split each scene’s 100100 independent 10710^{7}-history runs into a 5×1085\times 10^{8}-history reference and a sequence of MC budgets that grows to 5×1085\times 10^{8} histories. MC matches log10\log_{10} relative L2L_{2} at a median 9.4×103×9.4\times 10^{3}\times (interquartile range 4.9×1034.9\times 10^{3}–2.3×1042.3\times 10^{4}); for log10\log_{10} SSIM, 3232 of 5050 scenes remain unmatched at the largest budget (≈4.7×104×{\approx}4.7\times 10^{4}\times), and extrapolating each scene’s error curve by at most one order of magnitude gives a median of 6.4×104×6.4\times 10^{4}\times.

On EU-DEMO, MC matches the operator’s norm error only with a weight window, and even with one it misses the operator’s log10\log_{10} SSIM on every one of the 2424 scenes within the measured budgets (Table 16). We run three MC variants on 2424 scenes and count the weight-window generation cost where it applies. Without a window, MC does not match the operator within 10710^{7} histories on any scene. A cheap FW-CADIS window lets MC match log10\log_{10} relative L2L_{2} at 1.6×103×1.6\times 10^{3}\times the operator’s cost, but all 2424 scenes still miss its log10\log_{10} SSIM. The reference’s own FW-CADIS→\toMAGIC window also reaches the norm target, but building it takes ≈2,000{\approx}2{,}000 core-hours per scene, which lifts the end-to-end factor to 2.2×105×2.2\times 10^{5}\times. On every task, matching the dim-region structure measured by log10\log_{10} SSIM costs MC more than matching the norm.

For the MAGIC SSIM estimate, we extrapolate each scene’s error curve through its last two measured budgets by at most 1.51.5 orders of magnitude in particle count. Twenty scenes cross within this range; the remaining four are counted as lying above this range when computing the median over all 2424 scenes.

Appendix I Scope and In-Distribution Boundary

Which transport problems suit PTNO.

PTNO targets transport problems where low-order models fail and converged MC is expensive. In optically thick media with smooth coefficients, near-isotropic scattering, and clear scale separation, diffusion or low-order moment equations are accurate and a learned surrogate offers little. Our settings violate these conditions in different ways. The radiative-transfer datasets sample the Henyey–Greenstein asymmetry over nearly its whole range together with piecewise or shape-wise varying coefficients, so much of the training distribution is strongly anisotropic and has sharp interfaces. The neutronics settings are deep-shielding problems whose reference flux spans about 1010 (spherical tokamak) and 1717 (EU-DEMO) orders of magnitude (Table 18), hard enough that the EU-DEMO reference itself needs FW-CADIS and MAGIC weight windows. The cost accounting of Appendix H gives the practical criterion: the surrogate pays off most where the dim tail of the solution is expensive for MC to converge.

What the training designs vary.

Every held-out configuration is a fresh draw from the same design as the training set (Table 17), so all reported accuracy is interpolation within a parameterized family. The axes behave differently at the boundary. Coefficient ranges (σt\mathbf{\sigma}_{t}, cc, gg) and source parameters form a soft boundary: the solution depends smoothly on them, so a query just outside the sampled range is a mild extrapolation, which we do not evaluate. Geometry families form a hard boundary: within a family, geometry is parameterized and covered by the design, but a different machine, a new port, or a component absent from training is out of distribution. For EU-DEMO the family is a single fixed geometry.

Physical realism of the radiative-transfer designs.

The radiative-transfer designs are broader than any single application; the 3D fluence design carries the high-dynamic-range case on the radiative-transfer side, reproducing the dynamic range of the spherical tokamak. Extinction, albedo, and phase-function ranges are the physically admissible ranges used in participating-media simulation and rendering; cloud albedo, for example, lies close to 11, inside our range. The spatially varying fields combine localized structures, multiple scales, and sharp interfaces rather than one empirical distribution. Table 18 shows that a synthetic 3D fluence reference spans about 1010 orders of magnitude, as many as a spherical-tokamak reference and fewer than EU-DEMO (about 1717), while far-field radiance spans only about 33. Far-field radiance is therefore not a high-dynamic-range stress test; we use it for the label-noise and allocation studies because it is the one setting where converged references for thousands of training scenes are affordable.

Measured data.

Dense, full-field measurements are not available for either domain. No operating fusion power plant provides energy-resolved neutron fields under reactor conditions, and existing detectors give sparse readings with instrument-specific energy responses. Light-transport datasets provide images or sparse radiometry rather than full transport fields with the geometry, material, and illumination specifications needed for pointwise validation. Our evaluation is therefore simulation-based, as is standard in shielding and reactor design.

Appendix J Cross-Resolution Evaluation and Multi-Resolution Training

Single-resolution training supports native FNO inference on nearby meshes. On EU-DEMO, accuracy holds from 0.5×0.5\times to 1×1\times the training resolution and degrades moderately at 2×2\times; on far-field radiance, a native forward at 2×2\times outperforms low-resolution prediction followed by upsampling.

Far-field radiance.

We train at 40×8040{\times}80 and evaluate one earlier single-seed checkpoint, trained on 128128-SPP labels, on 100100 held-out scenes. At 80×16080{\times}160, native inference reaches log10\log_{10} SSIM 0.9310.931, compared with 0.9010.901 for block-replicating the 40×8040{\times}80 prediction. The native forward also lowers linear rel. L2L_{2} from 0.1650.165 to 0.1390.139. The five-seed checkpoints of Table 2 reach log10\log_{10} SSIM 0.8969±0.00300.8969\pm 0.0030 at 120×240120{\times}240, three times the training resolution per axis, against 0.9165±0.00400.9165\pm 0.0040 on the training grid.

EU-DEMO.

We train at 140×73×146140{\times}73{\times}146 and evaluate the five main-table seeds at 0.5×0.5\times, 1×1\times, and 2×2\times resolution, scoring only cells where the reference is measured (42.6%42.6\%, 45.4%45.4\%, and 46.6%46.6\% of the mesh). log10\log_{10} SSIM is 0.7895±0.00400.7895\pm 0.0040 at 0.5×0.5\times, 0.7923±0.00160.7923\pm 0.0016 at the training mesh, and 0.7181±0.00160.7181\pm 0.0016 at 2×2\times; the supports differ slightly between grids. At 5×5\times (700×365×730700{\times}365{\times}730, the reference’s native mesh, 49.1%49.1\% measured) log10\log_{10} rel. L2L_{2} stays at 0.0844±0.00040.0844\pm 0.0004, while log10\log_{10} SSIM falls to 0.5441±0.00060.5441\pm 0.0006: its 1111-cell window spans one fifth of the physical extent per axis that it spans at the training mesh, so the two SSIM values measure structure at different physical scales.

Mixed-resolution training at a tenfold grid step.

Adding 100100 high-resolution training scenes reduces the active-voxel log MAE (the mean absolute log10\log_{10} error over voxels whose reference flux is above the floor) of a direct forward pass on the 700×550×800700{\times}550{\times}800 native mesh from 5.365.36 to 2.362.36. Linear rel. L2L_{2} remains near one, so the added data reduces the severity of the native-scale collapse without establishing tenfold resolution invariance.

The mixed run reached epoch 1616 of 2020 under a six-hour limit. Its low-resolution accuracy matches the single-resolution baseline, and its direct native-scale prediction remains outside the training amplitude range. Nearby-mesh inference is reliable; a tenfold grid step requires an explicitly resolution-consistent representation.

Appendix K Radiative Transfer with Refractive and Reflective Interfaces

A fifth dataset adds glass, mirror, and matte objects to the 3D fluence task of Appendix E.2. Light that hits a glass object is bent into the geometric shadow behind it and partly reflected, a mirror folds the light field back on itself, and a matte object casts a soft shadow, so the target field is no longer a smooth function of the medium alone (). The PTNO recipe still learns this task from labels traced with 6464 Monte Carlo samples per voxel (SPP). We score a model by the SSIM between the log10\log_{10} of its predicted 3D fluence volume and the log10\log_{10} of a high-SPP Monte Carlo reference, computed on the volume itself, not on rendered images. On a held-out test set of 224224 scenes, scored only once after every design choice had been fixed, the final model reaches a log10\log_{10} SSIM of 0.9610.961. For scale, two independent Monte Carlo solutions of a different 224224-scene set from the same generator score 0.9970.997 against each other; this gives an empirical scale for reference noise, rather than a strict upper bound on model accuracy.

K.1 Scenes, Labels, and Reference

Each scene is a 3D fluence scene (background σt\mathbf{\sigma}_{t} and cc with 22–55 contrast solids, 11–33 point emitters, one Henyey–Greenstein gg) plus zero to three solid objects: spheres or axis-aligned boxes made of a dielectric with refractive index n∈[1.1,2.5]n\in[1.1,2.5], an ideal mirror, or a Lambertian (matte) surface with albedo cm∈[0.2,0.9]c_{\mathrm{m}}\in[0.2,0.9] (Table 21). Objects are opaque to the medium: the participating medium exists only outside them, and their interiors are a weak absorber (absorption coefficient σa=0.05\mathbf{\sigma}_{a}=0.05, no scattering), because a lossless glass box traps most interior directions and its interior fluence has no converged value. At an interface a photon is reflected or transmitted with the polarized Fresnel probability and refracted by Snell’s law, including total internal reflection; mirrors reflect with unit probability, and matte surfaces absorb a fraction 1−cm1-c_{\mathrm{m}} and re-emit the rest in a cosine-weighted direction.

Labels come from the Monte Carlo collision estimator of Appendix E.2 extended with analytic ray–sphere and ray–box intersections; the target is the per-voxel track-length fluence (the summed path length of photons inside a voxel, an unbiased estimate of fluence) on a 64364^{3} grid, divided by voxel volume and by total emitted power. The estimator was checked against Geant4 [53, 54] optical photons on the same analytic scenes: the two codes share neither the estimator nor the interface code, their difference falls as N−0.45N^{-0.45} over 2.5×1052.5\times 10^{5}–2×1062\times 10^{6} Geant4 photons with no plateau, and seven physics components isolated one at a time agree to 0.040.04–0.21%0.21\%. Training uses the first 10510^{5} scenes of a 10610^{6}-scene training set, each traced once at 6464 SPP, that is, 6464 photon paths per voxel of the 64364^{3} grid. Four held-out sets are used, all drawn from the same scene generator and disjoint from training and from each other: a 5050-scene set traced to 786,432786{,}432 SPP for monitoring during training; a 224224-scene stratified comparison set (77 interface compositions ×\times 3232 scenes: no object, one matte, one mirror, one dielectric with n<1.5n<1.5, one with n≥2.0n\geq 2.0, two dielectrics, three dielectrics) traced to 32,76832{,}768 SPP, on which we rank the variants; and two further 224224-scene sets with the same compositions and SPP but fresh random seeds, a selection set that scores each candidate once and is used only to choose among the final candidates, and a test set that scores each model once, after that choice. The label ceiling is one independent Monte Carlo solution of the stratified comparison set scored against another with the same metrics: log10\log_{10} SSIM 0.99680.9968 and log10\log_{10} rel. L2L_{2} 0.01130.0113. The final model remains about 0.030.03 below this empirical ceiling; this gap is larger than the reference-noise scale, although it does not certify every small difference between models.

K.2 Inputs, Model, and Protocol

The operator sees 2323 input channels, all computed from the scene parameters at the target resolution. The first 2121 channels comprise one emission grid, nine degree-00–22 source spherical-harmonic fields, extinction and albedo, four surface fields (refractive index, mirror mask, matte albedo, and signed distance), four polynomial embeddings of gg, and one asinh-encoded occluded direct-flux field. The remaining two tell the operator where the interfaces send light before any scattering: D0D_{0}, the direct flux with every interface treated as opaque, and RK​6R_{K6}, the extra energy delivered by up to six reflections or refractions; both are computed by a cheap deterministic ray tracer, encoded on a fixed log10\log_{10} scale, and also fed directly to the readout layer. Writing d=log10⁡max⁡(D0,10−8)d=\log_{10}\max(D_{0},10^{-8}), the final two channels are (d+4)/4(d+4)/4 and [log10⁡max⁡(D0+RK​6,10−8)−d]/4[\log_{10}\max(D_{0}+R_{K6},10^{-8})-d]/4, without fitted normalization. These channels are inputs computed from the scene, not labels: they contain no volume scattering or diffuse-surface bounce. The backbone is a 3D FNO (modes 32332^{3}, 88 layers, width 6464 for the final model) with a softplus head and PRel​L2\mathrm{PRel}L_{2} with η=2×10−6\eta=2\times 10^{-6} on the detached prediction. Every variant follows one protocol: the first 10510^{5} scenes seen once, 25,00025{,}000 AdamW updates at batch 44 with cosine decay from 3×10−33\times 10^{-3} to 10−710^{-7}, weight decay 10−310^{-3}, gradient clipping at 11, seeds 4242 and 4343, and the checkpoint at the end of training with no validation-based selection. The longer runs repeat the same 10510^{5} scenes two or four times with the schedule stretched accordingly, so they are compared only with each other. Metrics follow , with floor ϵ=3.28×10−7\epsilon=3.28\times 10^{-7} in the log10\log_{10} metrics. Linear relative L2L_{2} is not reported for this dataset: for a point source the cell average in the voxel that contains the emitter scales as h−2h^{-2} with the voxel width hh and has no continuum limit, and that single voxel carries 9898–100%100\% of every model’s squared error. We therefore rank in log10\log_{10} space and use the peak ratio, the predicted maximum over the reference maximum in each scene, to check that the source core is reproduced.

K.3 Results

PTNO learns this task from 6464-SPP labels to within 0.0350.035 of the label ceiling in log10\log_{10} SSIM (Table 22). The final model (width 6464, 88 layers, 10510^{5} updates) scores log10\log_{10} SSIM 0.96470.9647/0.96520.9652 on the stratified comparison set for seeds 4242/4343. We chose its seed-4343 checkpoint on the selection set; on the test set, scored once after that choice, it reaches log10\log_{10} SSIM 0.96110.9611 (median over scenes 0.97620.9762, 5th percentile 0.87600.8760), log10\log_{10} rel. L2L_{2} 0.07200.0720, and log10\log_{10} PSNR 38.138.1 dB. Across the seven interface compositions of the stratified comparison set, log10\log_{10} SSIM ranges from 0.9540.954/0.9550.955 (two dielectrics) to 0.9740.974/0.9740.974 (no object), and the worst single scene in every composition stays above 0.820.82. The source core is reproduced: the median over scenes of the peak ratio is 1.001.00/1.041.04. The remaining error sits in the dim regions behind glass objects, where the model over-predicts by 0.050.05–0.070.07 orders of magnitude at the median.

Training in the physical space matters here as on the other four datasets. With everything else fixed (same inputs, corpus, schedule, and seeds, at the 25,00025{,}000-update budget), replacing PTNO’s softplus head and PRel​L2\mathrm{PRel}L_{2} with a log10\log_{10} output trained by MSE lowers log10\log_{10} SSIM from 0.95030.9503/0.94900.9490 to 0.93910.9391/0.93640.9364. Table 23 repeats this comparison at the final model’s budget of 10510^{5} updates, again changing only the output head and the loss. The log10\log_{10}-output MSE model scores 0.0180.018/0.0190.019 below PTNO in log10\log_{10} SSIM on the stratified comparison set and 0.0170.017/0.0180.018 below on the test set, and an identity head trained with linear L2L_{2} collapses to a near-zero field. In the linear source core the log10\log_{10}-output model is closer to the reference than PTNO: its mean peak ratio is 0.9850.985/1.0161.016 against 1.7991.799/1.6271.627, and its core error is lower. These means keep every scene, and the PTNO seed-4242 core error of 1.1551.155 is carried by one three-dielectric scene (median over scenes 0.0680.068); the two seeds do not settle whether PTNO systematically overshoots the peak. Neither component works alone at this budget. With PRel​L2\mathrm{PRel}L_{2} but an identity head the model collapses to a near-zero field like the linear-L2L_{2} model, and with a softplus head but a per-sample relative L2L_{2} loss it outputs, in every scene, a constant at the head’s lower bound.

K.4 Limitations

All numbers in this section are two seeds of one from-scratch recipe with end-of-training checkpoints, not the five seeds of Table 2. The loss comparison of Table 22 was run at the 25,00025{,}000-update budget; Table 23 repeats it at 10510^{5} updates. The training corpus is fixed at 10510^{5} scenes because the two interface input channels are precomputed and stored for each training scene, so the dim-region bias reported here is the current state, not a floor. Linear relative L2L_{2} and cross-resolution evaluation are not reported, because the cell average in the voxel that contains a point emitter scales as h−2h^{-2} and has no continuum limit. The estimator and Geant4 share the same simplification of total internal reflection, so their agreement does not test that approximation.
